claims.text: The Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy can be produced by additive manufacturing with dual nanoprecipitates.
The dual nanoprecipitates provide a 300–400 MPa strength improvement over cast or wrought versions of the alloy.
High-temperature oxidation induces localized elemental redistribution in the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy.
Oxidation enriches Cr and Ti at nanoprecipitate/matrix interfaces and oxide interfaces.
Interfacial enrichment of Cr and Ti may enhance formation of a protective oxide scale.
Exposure at approximately 1000°C in air is an appropriate oxidation intervention for the proposed study.
Varying oxidation duration can capture early and later stages of oxidation.
Nanoprecipitates and their interfaces with the matrix are the structural mediators of the proposed oxidation response.
Atomic diffusion during high-temperature exposure causes elemental redistribution.
Cr and Ti are oxidation-resistant elements in the relevant alloy context.
Segregation of Cr and Ti to nanoprecipitate interfaces and the oxide/matrix boundary facilitates formation of a dense protective oxide scale.
Atom Probe Tomography can reveal sub-nanometer-scale elemental composition gradients in the oxidized alloy.
Oxidized samples will show higher local Cr and Ti concentrations around nanoprecipitates than an unoxidized control.
Observed elemental segregation will correlate with improved oxidation resistance.
Unoxidized additively manufactured samples have a relatively uniform elemental distribution within the nanoprecipitates.
Secondary phases or minor elements may affect the oxidation behavior.
Ex situ Atom Probe Tomography can provide three-dimensional elemental maps at sub-nanometer resolution at nanoprecipitates and their interfaces.
Failure to detect statistically significant Cr or Ti enrichment in oxidized samples relative to the unoxidized control would falsify the proposed redistribution hypothesis.
